name: Software change delivery: one user story from refinement to verified release
summary: This process takes one user story or small change in a product engineering team from backlog refinement to a verified production release. The product owner, developers, a code reviewer, a designer for some stories, a tester, a release engineer and a change manager each handle it, and some changes also need a security review. Hands-on work is a small share of the elapsed time: the story waits for refinement and sprint planning, for reviewers, for testers, for the release train and for the weekly change board. Rework loops come from failed builds, review comments, defects found in testing and the occasional failed deployment.

baseline.org_archetype: A product engineering group of about 150 people in 18 Scrum teams inside a 1,500-employee company, with two-week sprints, pull request reviews, continuous integration, a shared QA function, a two-week release train and a weekly change advisory board.
baseline.notes: Represents common practice in established companies, which DORA's surveys placed mostly in the medium performance group; teams with continuous deployment and no change board run much faster.

unit_of_work: one user story or small change
trigger: A backlog item reaches the top of the product owner's list and is prepared for refinement.
end_state: The change is live in production, verified and the story is closed; or the story is dropped.

volume.seasonality: Fewer releases during year-end change freezes and holiday periods.

evidence.note: 18 teams finishing about 8 to 12 stories per two-week sprint gives roughly 300 to 430 stories a month. Author estimate.

produces.object: change record with approvals and test evidence

evidence.note: Computer systems analyst median used as a stand-in for product owners in IT product teams. systems.name: Work tracker (backlog, sprint board, story records)
Test case management and defect tracking
Team wiki for specifications and release notes

steps.name: Prepare story for refinement
steps.description: The product owner takes a request or roadmap item from the backlog, writes it as a user story with acceptance criteria, attaches screenshots or customer evidence, and flags open questions for the team.

evidence.note: Product owner accountability for backlog items is in the Scrum Guide; times are author estimates.

steps.name: Refine and estimate with the team
steps.description: In the weekly refinement session the developers, tester and product owner discuss the story, split it if large, agree acceptance criteria and estimate it in story points. The touch time is the team's combined time on this story.

error.defect_description: Hidden complexity missed in the estimate.

next.condition: questions or split needed, back to product owner

evidence.note: Refinement adds detail, order and size (Scrum Guide); shares and times are author estimates.

steps.name: Design the user interface
steps.description: The UX designer sketches the flow, builds mock-ups or a clickable prototype, checks it with the product owner and sometimes with users, and attaches the final design to the story.

error.defect_description: Design misses an edge case found in testing.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common practice in product engineering teams using two-week sprints, 2019 to 2022.

steps.name: Plan story into a sprint
steps.description: At sprint planning the team compares its capacity with the ordered backlog and commits to a set of stories; this story is either taken into the sprint or left for a later one. The touch time is the team's share of planning time.

evidence.note: Sprints of one month or less; two-week sprints and the deferral share are author estimates.

steps.name: Pick up story and plan the approach
steps.description: A developer moves the story to in progress, reads the design and code involved, and notes the technical approach and tasks, sometimes after a short discussion with a senior colleague.

error.defect_description: Approach conflicts with other work in progress.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common practice in product engineering teams using two-week sprints, 2019 to 2022.

steps.name: Write code and unit tests
steps.description: The developer creates a branch, writes the change and its unit tests, runs them locally, and pushes commits. Larger stories take several days of interrupted work alongside meetings and support duties.

error.defect_description: Functional defects or missed acceptance criteria.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common practice in product engineering teams using two-week sprints, 2019 to 2022.

steps.name: Run automated build and tests
steps.description: The continuous integration server builds the branch and runs unit, integration and static analysis checks, then reports pass or fail on the pull request.

evidence.note: Automated build on every push is described by Fowler; the failure share is an author estimate.

steps.name: Fix failing build or tests
steps.description: The developer reads the build log, reproduces the failure locally, fixes the code or reruns or repairs a flaky test, and pushes the corrected commits so the build runs again.

evidence.note: Fixing broken builds immediately is described by Fowler; times are author estimates.

steps.name: Open or update pull request
steps.description: The developer opens the pull request with a description, links the story, tags reviewers and posts in the team chat. After rework the same step updates the request and asks for another look.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common practice in product engineering teams using two-week sprints, 2019 to 2022.

steps.name: Peer code review
steps.description: A senior developer reads the diff, checks logic, tests, naming and security issues, runs it locally if needed, and approves or requests changes. Pull requests often wait hours for a reviewer who is busy with their own work.

control.basis: Peer review before merge: a second developer approves every change (branch protection), used to meet IT general control requirements for program changes

next.condition: approved but touches authentication, payments or personal data

evidence.note: Median time in review of a few hours at Meta (2021) and 60 minute review sessions (SmartBear) are stated; typical teams wait longer than Meta, so the wait is an author estimate, as is the 33% change request rate.

steps.name: Address review comments
steps.description: The developer replies to each comment, changes the code or explains the choice, and pushes new commits, which rerun the build.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common practice in product engineering teams using two-week sprints, 2019 to 2022.

steps.name: Security review
steps.description: An application security engineer reviews changes to authentication, payment or personal data handling against the secure coding standard and threat model, and approves or asks for fixes.

control.basis: Secure development policy: security review of changes to sensitive functions

evidence.note: Author estimate from common practice in product engineering teams using two-week sprints, 2019 to 2022.

steps.name: Merge and deploy to test environment
steps.description: The pull request is merged to the main branch and the pipeline deploys the build to the shared test environment, either at once or in a nightly job.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common practice in product engineering teams using two-week sprints, 2019 to 2022.

steps.name: Manual testing against acceptance criteria
steps.description: The QA analyst writes or updates test cases, tests the story in the test environment on the supported browsers or devices, tries edge cases, and logs defects with steps to reproduce.

error.defect_description: Defect missed in testing, found after release.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common practice in product engineering teams using two-week sprints, 2019 to 2022.

steps.name: Fix defects found in testing
steps.description: The developer reproduces each defect, fixes it, adds a test and pushes, which sends the change back through build, review and testing.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common practice in product engineering teams using two-week sprints, 2019 to 2022.

steps.name: Product owner accepts the story
steps.description: The product owner tries the feature in the test environment or sees it at the sprint review, compares it with the acceptance criteria and accepts it or asks for changes.

next.condition: does not meet the intent, rework

evidence.note: Inspection at the sprint review and the Definition of Done are in the Scrum Guide; shares and times are author estimates.

steps.name: Regression test the release candidate
steps.description: When the release branch is cut, QA runs the automated regression suite and a manual regression checklist on staging for all stories in the release. The touch time is this story's share.

next.condition: regression defect linked to this story

evidence.note: Release branches and tests on the release candidate are described; a two-week release train and the defect share are author estimates.

steps.name: Prepare change request and release notes
steps.description: The release engineer raises the production change record with the list of stories, test evidence, risk rating, deployment and back-out plan, and drafts the release notes.

error.defect_description: Missing test evidence or back-out plan.

evidence.note: RFC logging is an ITIL sub-process; the per-story share of effort is an author estimate.

steps.name: Change advisory board approval
steps.description: The change manager reviews the change record and presents it at the weekly change advisory board, where operations, security and business representatives check risk, timing and conflicts before approving.

control.basis: IT general controls over program change management (Sarbanes-Oxley section 404 for listed companies): production changes authorised before deployment

evidence.note: CAB assessment and change controls are described; DORA finds no evidence that external approval lowers change failure. Weekly cadence is an author estimate.

steps.name: Deploy to production
steps.description: In the approved window the release engineer runs the deployment pipeline, watches health checks and error rates, and rolls back if the release fails. Developers do not deploy to production themselves.

control.basis: IT general controls: separation between developers and those who move code to production

next.condition: deployment fails and is rolled back

evidence.note: Automated, staged deployment described by Google SRE; the failure share is an author estimate.

steps.name: Verify in production
steps.description: After the release the QA analyst runs smoke tests on the live system and checks monitoring dashboards and support channels for errors linked to the story.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common practice in product engineering teams using two-week sprints, 2019 to 2022.

steps.name: Roll back or prepare hotfix
steps.description: The developer, with the release engineer, decides whether to roll back or fix forward, writes and tests the hotfix on a branch, and gets a quick peer review.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common practice in product engineering teams using two-week sprints, 2019 to 2022.

steps.name: Emergency change approval
steps.description: The change manager convenes the emergency change board or a delegated approver by phone or chat, reviews the hotfix risk and back-out plan, and approves an out-of-cycle deployment.

control.basis: IT general controls: emergency changes approved by an emergency change board and reviewed after the fact

evidence.note: Emergency changes approved by an ECAB are described; times are author estimates.

steps.name: Close the story
steps.description: The product owner or developer updates the story to done, links the release, and the change record is closed after the post-implementation check.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common practice in product engineering teams using two-week sprints, 2019 to 2022.

exceptions.name: Story needs interface design
exceptions.description: The story goes to the UX designer before it can be planned.

exceptions.name: Deferred at sprint planning
exceptions.description: The story does not fit the sprint's capacity and waits for the next planning session.

exceptions.name: Defects found in testing
exceptions.description: QA or regression testing finds defects; the fix goes back through build, review and test.

exceptions.name: Security review
exceptions.description: Changes to authentication, payments or personal data need application security sign-off.

exceptions.name: Failed change in production
exceptions.description: The deployment fails or a defect appears after release; the team rolls back or hotfixes under an emergency change.

exceptions.name: Dropped
exceptions.description: The story is dropped at refinement or planning as no longer worth building.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from refinement start to verified production release
benchmarks.population: Product teams with two-week sprints, a release train and a weekly change board (composite estimate)

evidence.note: No opened source measures refinement-to-release time. Composite: about two weeks from refinement to the start of coding (weekly refinement, two-week sprint planning) plus two to three weeks from commit to production through review, testing, a two-week release train and a weekly change board. DORA's 2022 survey put 69% of respondents in its medium cluster; its lead time thresholds could not be read from the opened page.

benchmarks.unit: hours a change waits on reviewer action
benchmarks.population: Meta, early 2021 (slowest quartile up to a day longer)

benchmarks.unit: lines of code per review, minutes per session, share of defects found
benchmarks.population: SmartBear study of a Cisco programming team
DORA Accelerate State of DevOps survey 2022

pain_points.description: Pull requests wait for reviewers busy with their own work; overdue reviews slow delivery.
Stories wait for the next refinement session, sprint planning and release train, so batching adds weeks regardless of effort.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common practice in product engineering teams using two-week sprints, 2019 to 2022.

pain_points.description: The weekly change advisory board adds days without evidence of fewer failed changes.
Manual testing in a shared test environment queues behind other teams and finds defects late, sending work back through build and review.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common practice in product engineering teams using two-week sprints, 2019 to 2022.

pain_points.description: Unclear acceptance criteria cause re-refinement and late product owner rejections.

evidence.note: Author estimate from common practice in product engineering teams using two-week sprints, 2019 to 2022.

sources.title: The Scrum Guide (2020)
sources.supports: Sprints of one month or less; product backlog refinement breaks items down and adds detail and size; product owner orders the backlog; Definition of Done; sprint review and retrospective.

sources.title: Best practices for peer code review
sources.supports: From a study of a Cisco programming team: review 200 to 400 lines at a time, under 500 lines per hour, no more than 60 minutes per session; such reviews find 70% to 90% of defects.

sources.title: Improving code review time at Meta
sources.supports: Time in review is time a diff waits on reviewer action; median a few hours in early 2021, with the slowest quartile taking up to a day longer; a nudge bot cut average time in review by 7%.

sources.title: Nudge: accelerating overdue pull requests towards completion
sources.supports: Overdue pull requests slow development; in a randomised trial on 147 Microsoft repositories, reminders cut resolution time of overdue pull requests by 60% across 8,500 pull requests.

sources.title: Announcing the 2021 Accelerate State of DevOps report
sources.supports: Elite performers' lead time for changes fell from under one day to under one hour; high and elite performers were two thirds of respondents in 2021, while low and medium were 56% in 2019.

sources.title: 2022 Accelerate State of DevOps report now out
sources.supports: In 2022 the medium cluster held 69% of respondents and low performers rose from 7% to 19%; no elite cluster emerged.

sources.title: Capabilities: streamlining change approval
sources.supports: Heavyweight external change approval slows delivery and no evidence links it to lower change fail rates; peer review recommended to meet segregation of duties.

sources.title: Change Management (ITIL)
sources.supports: RFC logging and pre-evaluation, assessment by the change manager or the change advisory board, emergency changes via an emergency CAB, pre-authorised standard changes, deployment authorisation, post implementation review.

sources.title: Information technology general controls
sources.supports: Program change management controls are among the most common IT general controls.

sources.title: Continuous integration
sources.supports: Every push triggers an integration build and tests; a failed build is fixed right away; a ten minute commit build; slower test stages follow in a deployment pipeline; test environments mimic production.

sources.title: Release engineering (Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 8)
sources.supports: Automated builds and tests on each change, release branches, packaged artifacts, staged rollouts; frequent releases mean fewer changes between versions.

sources.title: May 2021 national occupational employment and wage estimates, United States
Employer costs for employee compensation, December 2021
sources.supports: Private industry wages and salaries were 70.5% of employer compensation costs (December 2021).

assumptions: Group sessions (refinement, sprint planning) are attributed to the developer role with the whole team's time on this story as touch time.
Regression testing, change preparation and change board time are shared across all stories in a release; the touch time is one story's share.
Time spent in the backlog before the story is selected for refinement is excluded; it can be months.
Two-week sprints, a two-week release train and a weekly change board are author choices representing common practice in established companies; teams with continuous deployment skip s17 to s19.
Combined failed-change share (failed deployments plus production defects) is about 11%, an author estimate.
DORA cluster thresholds for lead time could not be extracted from the report PDFs, so the cycle time benchmark is a tier C composite.
Loaded hourly cost = BLS May 2021 median wage x 1.42 benefits factor (ECEC December 2021) x 1.15 overhead factor.
